bridges.mechanism: A spike in attacks causes immediate port closures, shipping delays and higher insurance for high-value hardware shipments (GPUs, racks), prompting investors and operators to postpone or cancel capital-intensive AI infrastructure deployments.
A surge in attacks on commercial shipping lifts freight and insurance costs and triggers near-term energy and consumer-price rises, causing markets to revise upward expected central-bank tightening.

A spike in hostile incidents against ships in regional chokepoints raises insurance and rerouting costs, creates immediate physical and logistical bottlenecks for oil and refined product shipments, and thereby increases near‑term energy price and supply pressure.

A spike in attacks raises marine insurance rates, forces rerouting to longer/less-secure shipping lanes and increases lead times for server and electrical equipment deliveries, prompting investors and developers to delay or cancel planned AI data‑center capex.

Significant redeployment of Western naval and surveillance assets to Middle Eastern chokepoints reduces available deterrent and ISR capacity in the European/Black Sea area, creating operational opportunity for increased Russian cross‑border probes and local kinetic incidents.

Increased outages at export and energy infrastructure produce local power disruptions and sharp short-term spikes in electricity costs that force data centers to curtail training runs and delay model development cycles.

Sustained increases in outages of oil export pipelines and terminals create prolonged supply-driven inflationary pressure that leads central banks to raise policy interest rates within the policy horizon.

Frequent outages at Middle Eastern energy facilities shrink global spare capacity and raise the strategic value of inflicting or denying energy output, incentivizing Russian actors to escalate strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure to maximize leverage while markets are tight.
Increases in physical oil export flows through the chokepoints raise global supply availability and directly put downward pressure on benchmark crude prices.

A sustained reduction in crude and product volumes transiting the chokepoints directly lowers global available supply and spare capacity, producing acute upward pressure on energy commodity prices that affects the Russia–Ukraine theater.

Higher oil export volumes stabilize regional fuel and electricity supplies and prices, reducing operational energy costs and enabling energy‑intensive AI training and inference workloads to proceed at prior or expanded rates.

Higher risk premia increase the cost of capital and lower expected returns, causing venture and corporate financiers to scale back or delay funding for frontier AI research, model training and infrastructure projects.
An elevated market risk premium in oil and shipping markets triggers flight-to-quality portfolio flows into benchmark sovereign bonds, increasing demand and depressing long-term government yields.

A rising geopolitical risk premium increases perceived project and financing risk and borrowing costs, directly reducing the rate at which capital is committed to large, capital‑intensive AI infrastructure projects.
A rise in cross‑border kinetic incidents increases global risk aversion and safe‑haven flows into core sovereign bonds, raising demand and thus lowering long‑term benchmark yields.

A spike in cross‑border incidents around the Russia–Ukraine front prompts NATO/partner navies to reassign ships and carrier strike groups to European waters and heightened patrols near the Black/ Baltic Seas, reducing the aggregate deployed assets and patrol intensity available for Middle East chokepoints.

Attacks on energy infrastructure disrupt power/communications and force reallocation of technical staff and budgets to emergency restoration, degrading organizations' ability to operate and maintain AI safety monitoring and mitigation systems.
Direct strikes on production, refining or storage physically remove barrels from available supply and raise near‑term supply‑risk premia in crude markets, driving benchmark oil prices up.

Sustained attacks degrading Russian energy production and export capacity force importers to source incremental crude and products from Gulf producers, increasing volumes transiting Middle East chokepoints as shipments are rerouted to compensate for lost Russian exports.

Wider operational use of long‑range unmanned strike systems accelerates deployment of embedded autonomy and remote-control software, increasing opportunities for malfunctions, misuse, and cyber exploitation that produce AI-related incidents.

Improved long‑range strike drone capability raises the probability of disruptive attacks on offshore platforms, tankers or remote facilities, increasing market supply risk premia and pushing crude prices higher.

Improved long‑range UAS operational experience and hardware from the Russia–Ukraine context are transferred (via arms sales, third‑party brokers, or imitation) to regional state and non‑state actors, enabling more frequent remote strikes and interdictions against commercial vessels and maritime infrastructure in chokepoint areas.

Accelerated deployment and demonstrated effectiveness of long‑range drones generate procurement and private‑sector demand for improved autonomy, perception and targeting models, directly accelerating AI development efforts focused on those capabilities.

Intense diplomatic signaling and allied coordination over the conflict drive governments to adopt stricter national-security‑oriented export controls and compliance requirements affecting AI development and deployment.

Coordinated diplomatic pressure and sanctions campaigns tied to the war prompt governments and blocs to adopt export controls, licensing requirements and tighter oversight of AI/compute transfers, directly increasing regulatory pressure on AI development and deployment.
Rising energy prices and supply constraints raise the marginal cost of large-scale GPU/cloud training, prompting firms to delay or scale down frontier model training and slow deployment schedules.
Sustained energy price and supply stress feeds through to higher headline inflation and inflation expectations, prompting markets to reprice and expect a tighter path for short‑term policy rates.

Heightened global energy price and supply stress raises the insured value and perceived exposure of shipments and terminal operations passing through chokepoints, driving up insurance costs and an observable risk premium embedded in oil and shipping prices.

Sustained spikes and volatility in energy prices raise expected operating costs and insurance/risk premia for energy‑intensive data centers, causing investors to delay, downsize or cancel capital commitments to AI infrastructure.
Sharp increases in energy costs lead enterprises to cut nonessential compute workloads and throttle training/inference jobs to control bills, reducing near‑term commercial cloud capacity utilization.

Rapid breakthroughs in frontier AI increase market expectations for medium-term productivity and growth (and associated inflation), leading investors to require higher long-term sovereign yields to compensate for anticipated higher real rates and inflation risk.

Accelerated frontier AI development shortens timelines for deployable maritime ISR and autonomous platforms, prompting states and coalitions to increase patrols and asset deployments to exploit or counter new capabilities.

Faster frontier AI development produces better perception, autonomy and sensor-fusion models that can be integrated into long‑range UAVs and loitering munitions, rapidly increasing their operational range, endurance and strike effectiveness.
Faster development of frontier models increases the number and size of training runs and expanded inference experimentation, directly raising demand for high-performance compute resources.

A sustained surge in capital flowing into frontier AI raises near-term aggregate demand and labor/capital utilization (through large cloud/spend and hiring), which pushes up inflation and money-market indicators and causes markets to price in higher expected policy rates.

Higher financial inflows into frontier AI projects translate into concrete purchases and commitments for GPUs, servers and data-center construction, driving capital allocation to infrastructure providers.
Increased funding enables more teams and experiments to run large-scale training and inference workloads, raising immediate utilization of compute capacity.

Improved AI safety and mitigation capacity (detection, response tooling, skilled operators) is integrated into oil-export control and cyberdefense systems, directly reducing successful AI-enabled intrusions and thus outage frequency.

Rises in AI-related hacks, misuses and available offensive models enable actors to weaponize autonomous systems and cyber tools against ships and port systems, directly increasing hostile incidents at sea.

A rising rate of AI‑related incidents (misattribution, autonomous misfires, or cyber‑spoofing) generates immediate interstate accusations and demands for de‑escalatory measures, prompting increased external diplomatic signaling and pressure on the belligerents.
A rise in high-profile safety or misuse incidents prompts investigations, hearings and emergency rulemaking that escalate formal regulatory scrutiny and enforcement pressure on AI actors.

A material tightening of enforceable AI regulation raises compliance costs and slows AI-driven investment and hiring, reducing near-term inflationary pressure and causing markets to lower their expected future policy-rate path.

Stricter, enforceable export controls and certification requirements for autonomous targeting and perception software constrain procurement, integration and international transfer of advanced AI modules, slowing the fielding of enhanced long‑range strike drones.

A sustained rise in global oil prices increases energy, cooling and logistics costs for hyperscalers and cloud providers, prompting reductions or rescheduling of high‑cost compute workloads and thereby slowing model training and feature rollouts.

Sustained higher crude prices raise the value of tanker cargoes and rents from seizing or interdicting shipments, increasing incentives for state proxies, militias and criminal groups to mount attacks on commercial shipping.
Elevated oil prices increase the payoff from sabotaging pipelines, terminals and export infrastructure, prompting more targeted attacks and rent-seeking disruptions of facilities.

Sustained higher crude prices increase the economic value of energy infrastructure and, through higher state and criminal rents, provide both the incentive and financing to mount attacks against production, storage and transport facilities in the theater.

A sustained increase in oil (and related energy/transport) prices raises operational costs for power‑intensive AI training and for moving hardware, causing firms to reduce or postpone large training runs and thereby cutting immediate compute demand.

A rise in policy interest rates raises the cost of borrowing and increases discount rates for investors and VC funds, causing immediate pull‑backs or down‑valuations of capital committed to high‑burn, long‑horizon frontier AI projects.
Tighter policy rates raise borrowing and hedging costs and reduce market liquidity, causing insurers, traders and investors to demand wider risk premia on oil and shipping exposures.

A rise in short-term policy rates depresses aggregate demand and freight/industrial activity within months, reducing near‑term energy consumption and easing price and supply pressure on energy markets.

Higher short‑term policy rates raise corporate borrowing costs and tighten working‑capital budgets, prompting enterprises to defer non‑critical cloud deployments and scale‑ups, which lowers near‑term cloud capacity utilization.

Stronger market expectations of higher future policy rates lead firms to reprioritise short‑term profitability over long, compute‑intensive R&D, delaying large training runs and hiring and thus slowing the pace of frontier model development.

Market expectations of tighter policy lead venture investors and corporate CFOs to reprice risk and conserve cash, directly slowing hiring, project starts and model development budgets in the near term.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields increase government debt service burdens and fiscal pressure, leading to budgetary constraints that delay rule‑making, reduce enforcement capacity, and blunt the scope/rigour of new AI regulatory initiatives.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase fiscal pressure and near‑term debt servicing costs, prompting some governments to defer naval deployments and maintenance, thereby reducing active maritime presence.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase discount rates and debt-servicing costs for long‑lived data‑centre and GPU‑farm projects, directly reducing the financial viability and therefore new investment into AI infrastructure.

A faster pace of AI development produces automated sensor‑to‑target analysis and decision‑support tools that shorten timelines for target discovery and engagement, enabling more frequent and precise strikes on energy production, storage and distribution nodes.

Sharp increases in observable demand for high-end compute (GPU/TPU orders, datacenter capacity bids) trigger policymakers to introduce or tighten export controls, procurement restrictions, and mandatory oversight of compute-intensive training to limit dual‑use risks.

Rising competition for limited compute capacity reallocates scarce secure, isolated testbeds and compute time away from safety evaluations toward commercial training runs, reducing the throughput of safety testing and remediation.

Higher multi‑tenant cloud utilization increases surface area for misconfiguration, noisy‑neighbor failures, and lateral escalation, which directly raises the short‑term rate of outages, data exposures and abuse events involving deployed models.

A jump in cloud utilization that substitutes for firms' own hardware investment reduces aggregate corporate capex and long‑dated borrowing needs, weakening demand for credit and placing modest downward pressure on long-term sovereign yields.

Higher cloud capacity utilization by military and intelligence users supports near‑real‑time geospatial data processing and shared situational awareness, reducing misidentification and uncoordinated movements that lead to cross‑border armed incidents.

Sharper regulatory action or enforcement against AI deployment raises compliance costs and delays hiring/investment in the tech sector, dampening growth and inflation forecasts and leading markets to lower expected future policy rates.

Stronger AI export controls, sanctions and enforcement actions trigger formal diplomatic démarches, multilateral coordination efforts and public pressure campaigns aimed at restricting adversaries' access to critical technologies relevant to the conflict.

Visible, large investments into AI infrastructure lower marginal training costs and signal commercial viability, directly attracting additional finance into frontier model R&D and commercialization by improving expected returns on upstream bets.

A sustained rise in capital directed to AI data centers and related fixed assets leads firms and municipalities to issue more long-dated debt and reallocates investor demand away from sovereign bonds, exerting upward pressure on benchmark long-term yields.

Elevated investment spending in AI infrastructure boosts near‑term aggregate demand and input-price pressures (construction, electricity, semiconductors), prompting markets to revise up expected central-bank tightening over the policy horizon.

Increased investment in AI/compute infrastructure funds procurement and deployment of maritime ISR, long‑endurance drones and autonomous surface/underwater craft by states and private security firms, enabling more persistent patrols and higher deployed naval/maritime security presence around chokepoints.

Increased capital directed to AI infrastructure enables procurement of high‑end accelerators, datacenter capacity and MLOps services used by defense contractors and startups, accelerating development, autonomy and operational deployment of long‑range unmanned strike systems and swarm coordination.

Maritime attack frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which hostile incidents (attacks, strikes, interdictions) occur against commercial ships and maritime infrastructure in the region.

nodes.label: Non-state offensive capability
nodes.description: The aggregate kinetic and logistical capability of irregular or proxy forces to carry out maritime or energy-infrastructure attacks.

nodes.label: Naval/military presence level
nodes.description: The aggregate deployed military assets, patrol intensity and readiness in maritime areas affecting commercial transit.

nodes.label: Protective window duration
nodes.description: Average length of time per transit that commercial vessels receive active defensive coverage or escort protection.

nodes.label: Shipping rerouting burden
nodes.description: Average additional distance, time and operational burden imposed on commercial shipping due to avoidance of high-risk routes.

nodes.label: Chokepoint transit volume
nodes.description: Volume of commercial maritime traffic transiting critical maritime chokepoints per unit time.

nodes.label: Infrastructure outage rate
nodes.description: Frequency and duration-weighted rate of outages and service interruptions across oil export pipelines, terminals and related facilities.

nodes.label: Oil export flow
nodes.description: Volume of crude oil and refined product exports moving through regional routes and facilities per unit time.

nodes.label: Oil export capacity
nodes.description: Maximum technically available throughput of export infrastructure (pipelines, terminals, tanker availability) absent operational disruptions.

nodes.label: Market risk premium
nodes.description: Incremental price component embedded in oil and shipping markets that reflects perceived geopolitical and conflict risk.

nodes.label: Oil price level
nodes.description: prevailing market price level for benchmark crude oil relevant to global trade and regional export economics.

nodes.label: Insurance and security premium
nodes.description: Average insurance, armed-guard and security surcharge applied to vessels and cargo operating in the affected maritime zone.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: Short-term variability and uncertainty in commodity, freight and financial markets driven by the maritime-security situation.

nodes.label: Diplomatic engagement intensity
nodes.description: Frequency, scale and depth of diplomatic interactions, negotiations and mediation efforts aimed at conflict containment or resolution.

nodes.label: Diplomatic leverage balance
nodes.description: Net capacity of diplomatic incentives, sanctions and bargaining power to influence actors' choices toward escalation or restraint.

nodes.label: Great-power competition intensity
nodes.description: Degree of strategic rivalry and external-state involvement that shapes incentives, support networks and constraints in the regional system.

Border incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency per unit time of armed or kinetic incidents crossing or occurring at international land or maritime boundaries adjacent to the combat zone.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure strike rate
nodes.description: The rate at which attacks are directed against energy production, refining, storage, and distribution facilities.

nodes.label: Transport infrastructure strike rate
nodes.description: The rate of attacks on transport nodes and lines including rail, road corridors, and terminals affecting civilian and military movement.

nodes.label: Long‑range unmanned strike capability
nodes.description: The aggregate operational capacity and effectiveness of unmanned aerial systems to conduct long‑range reconnaissance and strike missions.

nodes.label: Energy infrastructure damage level
nodes.description: The accumulated physical degradation and functional loss across energy assets and networks resulting from attacks and disruptions.

nodes.label: Seasonal energy vulnerability
nodes.description: The degree to which heating and electrical demand, supply shortfalls, and infrastructure fragility increase exposure during cold seasons.

nodes.label: Fuel reserve level
nodes.description: The available stock of refined and crude fuel held in storage that can be mobilized for civilian and military use.

nodes.label: Civilian harm and displacement rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of civilian casualties, injuries, and population displacement attributable to hostilities and infrastructure disruption.

nodes.label: Transport network operability
nodes.description: The functional availability and throughput capacity of key transport routes and modal nodes for movement of people and goods.

nodes.label: Diplomatic pressure intensity
nodes.description: The intensity and frequency of external political signaling, demands, and incentives applied to influence operational decisions in the conflict zone.

nodes.label: Political signaling polarity
nodes.description: The degree of divergence and oppositional tone among influential political messages and public stances regarding conduct and restraints in the conflict.

nodes.label: Security partnership cohesion
nodes.description: The extent of consensus, coordinated action, and mutual support among cooperative security actors responding to cross‑border incidents and escalation.

nodes.label: Systemic escalation risk
nodes.description: The perceived probability and imminence that localized hostilities will broaden in scope, intensity, or geographic reach into a larger confrontation.

nodes.label: Airspace incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of detected incursions, near‑misses, interceptions, and unidentified aerial events affecting controlled airspace over and near the conflict area.

nodes.label: Humanitarian response capacity
nodes.description: The available stock of shelters, medical services, logistics, and relief resources to absorb civilian needs generated by hostilities and infrastructure loss.

nodes.label: Energy price and supply pressure
nodes.description: The level of market and supply‑chain stresses reflected in energy commodity price volatility and constraints that affect economic and policy choices.

Frontier model capability
nodes.description: The aggregate technical performance and generalization power of cutting‑edge AI models measured across benchmarks, scale, and emergent abilities.

nodes.label: Development pace
nodes.description: The speed at which new frontier AI models and features are researched, trained, validated and deployed into production environments.

nodes.label: Investment flow
nodes.description: The rate and volume of financial capital directed into frontier AI research, model training, infrastructure and commercialization.

nodes.label: Talent concentration
nodes.description: The available stock and geographic/organizational concentration of skilled researchers, engineers and technical managers in frontier AI.

nodes.label: Deployment incentives
nodes.description: The strength of economic and strategic incentives pushing actors to release, monetize or scale AI systems rapidly.

nodes.label: Safety mitigation capacity
nodes.description: The system's technical and operational ability to prevent, detect and mitigate hazards from AI models, including tooling, processes and skilled personnel.

nodes.label: Incident frequency
nodes.description: The rate at which safety, security or misuse events involving AI occur, including hacks, misuses, and unintended harmful outputs.

nodes.label: Adversarial activity level
nodes.description: The intensity and sophistication of malicious, hostile or military exploitation of AI capabilities by non‑benign actors.

nodes.label: Regulatory stringency
nodes.description: The strength, scope and enforceability of legal and regulatory requirements targeting AI development, deployment and risk mitigation.

nodes.label: Public trust level
nodes.description: The aggregate public confidence in AI systems and organisations deploying them, reflecting perceived safety, fairness and accountability.

nodes.label: Media attention level
nodes.description: The intensity and persistence of news, commentary and investigative coverage focused on AI risks, incidents and governance debates.

nodes.label: Reputational risk
nodes.description: The perceived exposure and vulnerability of AI developers and deployers to reputational damage from incidents, controversies or regulatory findings.

nodes.label: Infrastructure capacity
nodes.description: The available compute, data, storage and operational infrastructure that supports large‑scale model training, serving and experimentation.

nodes.label: Governance coordination
nodes.description: The degree of cross‑jurisdictional and cross‑sector alignment, information‑sharing and joint policy action on AI governance and controls.

nodes.label: Technical transparency
nodes.description: The level of visibility into model architectures, training data, evaluation results and mitigation practices available to regulators, auditors and partners.

nodes.label: Automation adoption rate
nodes.description: The speed at which enterprises and workplaces integrate AI systems into production processes and job tasks.

Global crude oil price level
nodes.description: The prevailing market price level for crude oil across major benchmarks, measured continuously.

nodes.label: Oil supply disruption intensity
nodes.description: The magnitude and persistence of reductions or interruptions in oil production and logistics that constrain available supply.

nodes.label: Headline consumer inflation rate
nodes.description: The percentage change in a broad consumer price index (including all items) over a specified trailing period.

nodes.label: Core consumer inflation rate
nodes.description: The percentage change in consumer prices excluding volatile components (e.g., food and energy) over a specified trailing period.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Average medium-term inflation expected by households, firms, and markets as reflected in surveys and market prices.

nodes.label: Policy interest rate level
nodes.description: The current short-term policy interest rate set through the monetary policy framework that influences interbank rates.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: The market-implied or surveyed expected path of future policy interest rates over the policy horizon.

nodes.label: Long-term government bond yield
nodes.description: The prevailing yield on benchmark long-term sovereign debt instruments that sets the risk-free rate for the economy.

nodes.label: Corporate credit spread
nodes.description: The average premium corporate borrowers pay over benchmark sovereign yields, reflecting credit risk and liquidity conditions.

nodes.label: Mortgage interest rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing interest rate charged on new mortgage-originations, reflecting funding costs and credit conditions.

nodes.label: Sovereign debt service burden
nodes.description: The flow measure of government resources (relative to revenues or GDP) required to service interest and principal on public debt.

nodes.label: Fiscal deficit ratio
nodes.description: The government budget shortfall measured as a share of GDP or revenues over a fiscal period, indicating net fiscal borrowing needs.

nodes.label: Market liquidity conditions
nodes.description: The ease, depth, and cost of transacting in financial markets, including bid-ask spreads and market depth across asset classes.

nodes.label: Market risk premia level
nodes.description: The prevailing compensation investors demand for bearing broad market and asset-specific risk above risk-free returns.

nodes.label: Real household consumption growth
nodes.description: The rate of change in inflation-adjusted household spending on goods and services over a specified period.

nodes.label: Corporate financing conditions
nodes.description: The combined availability, cost, and terms of external finance for firms, including issuance volumes, spreads, and credit access.

AI development pace
nodes.description: The rate at which new AI models, capabilities and deployments are being created and pushed toward production.

nodes.label: Safety signaling intensity
nodes.description: The frequency and strength of public calls, warnings and moratoria advocating slowing or constraining AI progress.

nodes.label: AI compute demand
nodes.description: The flow rate of high-performance compute resources required for AI training and inference workloads across the economy.

nodes.label: High-performance hardware supply
nodes.description: The available stock of specialized compute hardware (e.g., accelerators, servers and related components) ready for deployment.

nodes.label: Cloud capacity utilization
nodes.description: The proportion of commercial cloud compute and storage capacity currently in use for enterprise and AI workloads.

nodes.label: In‑house infrastructure adoption
nodes.description: The share of organizations' AI compute needs met by internally owned or operated infrastructure rather than third‑party cloud services.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment toward AI
nodes.description: The collective market perception and risk appetite of investors specifically regarding AI‑linked assets and infrastructure investments.

nodes.label: AI‑related asset volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude of short‑term price swings in securities, instruments and valuations linked to AI technologies and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Data governance scrutiny
nodes.description: The level of regulatory, legal and public attention focused on data handling, sharing and privacy practices related to AI.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity incident rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of detected security breaches, data thefts and successful cyberattacks affecting AI systems and data holdings.

nodes.label: Regulatory policy pressure
nodes.description: The intensity and trajectory of formal policy measures, enforcement actions and legislative pressure targeting AI development and deployment.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tension level
nodes.description: The level of interstate strategic competition, trade frictions and geopolitical risk that affect technology cooperation and supply chains.

nodes.label: Capital flow to AI infrastructure
nodes.description: The monetary investment rate directed toward building, expanding or acquiring compute infrastructure, data centers and related assets.

nodes.label: Energy supply stress for data centers
nodes.description: The degree of pressure on electricity availability, reliability and price that constrains data center operations and siting decisions.

nodes.label: Semiconductor supply‑chain resilience
nodes.description: The robustness of upstream component production, logistics and manufacturing capacity to meet demand for AI‑oriented chips and equipment.

nodes.label: AI talent availability
nodes.description: The size and accessibility of the skilled labor pool capable of developing, deploying and securing advanced AI systems.

A rise in high-profile safety or misuse incidents prompts investigations, hearings and emergency rulemaking that escalate formal regulatory scrutiny and enforcement pressure on AI actors.

A material tightening of enforceable AI regulation raises compliance costs and slows AI-driven investment and hiring, reducing near-term inflationary pressure and causing markets to lower their expected future policy-rate path.

Stricter, enforceable export controls and certification requirements for autonomous targeting and perception software constrain procurement, integration and international transfer of advanced AI modules, slowing the fielding of enhanced long‑range strike drones.

A sustained rise in global oil prices increases energy, cooling and logistics costs for hyperscalers and cloud providers, prompting reductions or rescheduling of high‑cost compute workloads and thereby slowing model training and feature rollouts.

Sustained higher crude prices raise the value of tanker cargoes and rents from seizing or interdicting shipments, increasing incentives for state proxies, militias and criminal groups to mount attacks on commercial shipping.
Elevated oil prices increase the payoff from sabotaging pipelines, terminals and export infrastructure, prompting more targeted attacks and rent-seeking disruptions of facilities.

Sustained higher crude prices increase the economic value of energy infrastructure and, through higher state and criminal rents, provide both the incentive and financing to mount attacks against production, storage and transport facilities in the theater.

A sustained increase in oil (and related energy/transport) prices raises operational costs for power‑intensive AI training and for moving hardware, causing firms to reduce or postpone large training runs and thereby cutting immediate compute demand.

A rise in policy interest rates raises the cost of borrowing and increases discount rates for investors and VC funds, causing immediate pull‑backs or down‑valuations of capital committed to high‑burn, long‑horizon frontier AI projects.
Tighter policy rates raise borrowing and hedging costs and reduce market liquidity, causing insurers, traders and investors to demand wider risk premia on oil and shipping exposures.

A rise in short-term policy rates depresses aggregate demand and freight/industrial activity within months, reducing near‑term energy consumption and easing price and supply pressure on energy markets.

Higher short‑term policy rates raise corporate borrowing costs and tighten working‑capital budgets, prompting enterprises to defer non‑critical cloud deployments and scale‑ups, which lowers near‑term cloud capacity utilization.

Stronger market expectations of higher future policy rates lead firms to reprioritise short‑term profitability over long, compute‑intensive R&D, delaying large training runs and hiring and thus slowing the pace of frontier model development.

Market expectations of tighter policy lead venture investors and corporate CFOs to reprice risk and conserve cash, directly slowing hiring, project starts and model development budgets in the near term.

Rising long‑term sovereign yields increase government debt service burdens and fiscal pressure, leading to budgetary constraints that delay rule‑making, reduce enforcement capacity, and blunt the scope/rigour of new AI regulatory initiatives.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase fiscal pressure and near‑term debt servicing costs, prompting some governments to defer naval deployments and maintenance, thereby reducing active maritime presence.

Rising long-term sovereign yields increase discount rates and debt-servicing costs for long‑lived data‑centre and GPU‑farm projects, directly reducing the financial viability and therefore new investment into AI infrastructure.

A faster pace of AI development produces automated sensor‑to‑target analysis and decision‑support tools that shorten timelines for target discovery and engagement, enabling more frequent and precise strikes on energy production, storage and distribution nodes.

Sharp increases in observable demand for high-end compute (GPU/TPU orders, datacenter capacity bids) trigger policymakers to introduce or tighten export controls, procurement restrictions, and mandatory oversight of compute-intensive training to limit dual‑use risks.

Rising competition for limited compute capacity reallocates scarce secure, isolated testbeds and compute time away from safety evaluations toward commercial training runs, reducing the throughput of safety testing and remediation.

Higher multi‑tenant cloud utilization increases surface area for misconfiguration, noisy‑neighbor failures, and lateral escalation, which directly raises the short‑term rate of outages, data exposures and abuse events involving deployed models.

A jump in cloud utilization that substitutes for firms' own hardware investment reduces aggregate corporate capex and long‑dated borrowing needs, weakening demand for credit and placing modest downward pressure on long-term sovereign yields.

Higher cloud capacity utilization by military and intelligence users supports near‑real‑time geospatial data processing and shared situational awareness, reducing misidentification and uncoordinated movements that lead to cross‑border armed incidents.

Sharper regulatory action or enforcement against AI deployment raises compliance costs and delays hiring/investment in the tech sector, dampening growth and inflation forecasts and leading markets to lower expected future policy rates.

Stronger AI export controls, sanctions and enforcement actions trigger formal diplomatic démarches, multilateral coordination efforts and public pressure campaigns aimed at restricting adversaries' access to critical technologies relevant to the conflict.

Visible, large investments into AI infrastructure lower marginal training costs and signal commercial viability, directly attracting additional finance into frontier model R&D and commercialization by improving expected returns on upstream bets.

A sustained rise in capital directed to AI data centers and related fixed assets leads firms and municipalities to issue more long-dated debt and reallocates investor demand away from sovereign bonds, exerting upward pressure on benchmark long-term yields.

Elevated investment spending in AI infrastructure boosts near‑term aggregate demand and input-price pressures (construction, electricity, semiconductors), prompting markets to revise up expected central-bank tightening over the policy horizon.

Increased investment in AI/compute infrastructure funds procurement and deployment of maritime ISR, long‑endurance drones and autonomous surface/underwater craft by states and private security firms, enabling more persistent patrols and higher deployed naval/maritime security presence around chokepoints.

Increased capital directed to AI infrastructure enables procurement of high‑end accelerators, datacenter capacity and MLOps services used by defense contractors and startups, accelerating development, autonomy and operational deployment of long‑range unmanned strike systems and swarm coordination.
